item.title: Automating Kubernetes Deployments: From Git Push to Verification and Recovery
item.description:
The earlier Docker to Kubernetes guide introduced Pods, Deployments, and Services. The container cloud deployment walkthrough connected Dockerfile builds, registry uploads, and platform configuration. The CI/CD guide explained the pipeline concepts.

Once the application can be deployed manually, those steps can move into a pipeline. A code change can then trigger tests, an image build, deployment, and checks that detect a broken release.

The example follows a small Go service through this process. The order API only demonstrates an HTTP service; it does not process real orders or connect to a database.

1. Turn deployment into a sequence of checks

Manual releases often rely on judgments such as “this image should be current” or “the page loads, so the deployment probably worked.” A pipeline needs explicit inputs, outputs, and checks to make those decisions.

Stage Input → output Acceptance criteria On failure
Integration PR → checked commit Unit tests, static checks, Dockerfile build Block merge
Artifact build Main commit → image Build and push succeed, digest available Do not deploy
Preparation Digest + manifests → release plan API reachable, identity valid, permissions sufficient Preserve live version
Deployment Plan → new Pods Rolling update completes Collect evidence and attempt recovery
Acceptance Service → real responses Health, business smoke test, and source version match Restore previous Pod template
Observation Logs and metrics → release decision Errors, latency, and business indicators acceptable Stop promotion and follow recovery policy

The example uses GitHub Actions → GHCR → Kubernetes. Pull requests run checks; merging into main builds an image and deploys it to a dedicated demo-prod namespace. Keeping human approval makes this continuous delivery. Automatically deploying after the checks pass is continuous deployment.

You need an existing cluster, an application repository on GitHub, and an administrator who can initialize the namespace. Commands use Linux/Bash; Windows users can use WSL or Git Bash. Target nodes use linux/amd64. Cluster installation is covered in the earlier guide.

Check that each part of the system can reach the services it needs:

Connection Required conditions
Runner → GitHub, GHCR, and tool download endpoints Source checkout, tool installation, image upload
Runner → Kubernetes API Reachable kubeconfig endpoint and trusted TLS certificate
Kubernetes nodes → GHCR Registry connectivity and credentials for private images
Users → gateway → Service → Pods Working controller, DNS, TLS, and backend routing

A working kubectl connection does not mean the nodes can pull images, and logging the Runner into GHCR does not log the nodes in. GitHub-hosted Runners also cannot directly reach your computer’s 127.0.0.1 or a private corporate API. Private clusters need a dedicated Runner on a trusted network or an approved private connection.

The service exposes /healthz to check process health, /readyz to report whether it can receive traffic, and /version to return the Git SHA embedded during compilation. The health handlers have no external dependencies. If you add a database, design readiness around the workload so a shared database failure does not cause every instance to restart.

package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"sync/atomic"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)

var version = "dev"

func routes(ready *atomic.Bool) http.Handler {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "ok")
	})
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /readyz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if !ready.Load() {
			http.Error(w, "not ready", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
			return
		}
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "ready")
	})
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /version", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, version)
	})
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /{$}", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		fmt.Fprintln(w, "order-api is running")
	})
	return mux
}

func main() {
	var ready atomic.Bool
	ready.Store(true)
	server := &http.Server{
		Addr: ":8080", Handler: routes(&ready),
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
	}
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()
	go func() {
		if err := server.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
	}()
	<-ctx.Done()
	ready.Store(false)
	shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	if err := server.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
		log.Print(err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}

The service listens on the container’s network interfaces. On termination, it marks itself unready and waits for active requests to finish. A real application also needs to drain connections, handle long-lived connections, and coordinate background tasks. These settings alone cannot guarantee uninterrupted service.

package main

import (
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"sync/atomic"
	"testing"
)

func TestReleaseContract(t *testing.T) {
	var ready atomic.Bool
	handler := routes(&ready)
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		path   string
		ready  bool
		status int
		body   string
	}{
		{"/healthz", false, 200, "ok"},
		{"/readyz", false, 503, "not ready"},
		{"/readyz", true, 200, "ready"},
		{"/version", true, 200, version},
		{"/", true, 200, "order-api is running"},
	} {
		ready.Store(tc.ready)
		recorder := httptest.NewRecorder()
		handler.ServeHTTP(recorder, httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, tc.path, nil))
		if recorder.Code != tc.status || strings.TrimSpace(recorder.Body.String()) != tc.body {
			t.Errorf("%s ready=%v: status=%d body=%q", tc.path, tc.ready, recorder.Code, recorder.Body.String())
		}
	}
}

COPY go.mod main.go ./
ARG VERSION=dev
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -trimpath \

USER 65532:65532

The example uses only the standard library, so it needs no third-party modules or go.sum. Its runtime image has no shell. If the application later needs outbound HTTPS, timezone data, or dynamic libraries, add the required files or choose a suitable runtime image. Keep base images updated with security fixes and pin approved images by digest in production, since a version tag can still point to different content.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-api
  namespace: demo-prod
spec:
  replicas: 2
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  minReadySeconds: 5
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 180
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-api
    spec:
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: ghcr-read
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/arch: amd64
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 65532
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: order-api
          # Template placeholder; replaced locally with the release digest before apply.
          image: ghcr.io/your-owner/order-api:replace-before-apply
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: order-api-config-v1
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 128Mi
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 30
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10

APP_ENV demonstrates configuration injection without changing the service’s behavior. When changing configuration, create order-api-config-v2, update the Deployment reference, and keep the old object. An old template can then use the configuration it originally referenced when restored. Secrets also need a version strategy; do not put credentials in ConfigMaps.

Setting Release behavior
startupProbe Readiness and liveness do not run until startup succeeds
readinessProbe Unready Pods are excluded from normal ready Service backends
livenessProbe Repeated failures eventually trigger a container restart
minReadySeconds: 5 A new replica must remain ready before being considered available
maxUnavailable: 0 Planned updates do not deliberately reduce available replicas
maxSurge: 1 One extra update replica is allowed; spare capacity is needed
progressDeadlineSeconds: 180 Reports failed progress after the configured deadline

See the official probe documentation for the detailed behavior. Setting a progress deadline does not automatically restore the previous version. The workflow below handles recovery explicitly.

The diagram shows the ideal update order. In practice, node failures, capacity shortages, endpoint propagation delays, and application behavior can affect availability. Terminating Pods may still consume resources, temporarily pushing usage beyond the three active slots shown here.

The example first uses ClusterIP and port forwarding to check the application. To make it accessible to users, have the platform configure a Gateway/Ingress, DNS, and TLS. An Ingress object needs a running controller; a ClusterIP cannot be used as a public address.

4. Establish identities and release permissions

There are three separate credentials:

Credential Consumer Purpose Provisioning
GITHUB_TOKEN Build Job Publish to GHCR Job token with packages: write
ghcr-read Kubernetes nodes Pull a private image Administrator-created registry Secret
KUBE_CONFIG Deploy Job Update applications in demo-prod Restricted deployer kubeconfig

New GHCR packages are private by default. You can make a demonstration image public or configure private image access as shown below. CI’s write permission does not give the nodes read permission. See GitHub’s Container registry documentation.

# Also satisfy organizational SSO and package access policies.
read -r -p 'GHCR username: ' GHCR_USER
read -r -s -p 'GHCR read token: ' GHCR_READ_TOKEN

  --docker-password="$GHCR_READ_TOKEN"
unset GHCR_READ_TOKEN

Use an account that can access the target package and a classic PAT with read:packages. Organizational SSO and package policies may require further authorization. The initialization command briefly exposes the token in local process arguments, so run it in a controlled terminal. On shared hosts, use platform secret management or controlled Docker configuration imports. If the Secret already exists, rotate it through the platform’s approved process.

This Role cannot manage the cluster, change RBAC, or directly read Secrets. An identity allowed to modify workloads may still make a Pod mount Secrets from the namespace, though. Use a dedicated namespace, allow only trusted deployment code, and apply appropriate admission and workload identity policies. See Kubernetes RBAC.

Next, generate a short-lived kubeconfig for the exercise. Run the commands locally as an administrator connected to the intended cluster. They copy the endpoint and CA without copying the administrator’s credentials, and request a one-hour ServiceAccount token. The server determines its actual lifetime.

The authorization check should return yes. These commands assume a standard HTTPS endpoint and CA. If the platform requires proxies, a special TLS server name, or cloud authentication plugins, use a suitable restricted CI kubeconfig from the platform. Do not bypass certificate verification.

Create a production environment in the application repository’s Settings → Environments. Restrict deployments to main and configure approval if desired and supported. Add environment Secret KUBE_CONFIG containing this file. With an authenticated GitHub CLI:

1

gh secret set KUBE_CONFIG --env production < .deploy-local/ci.kubeconfig

Create an environment Variable named KUBECTL_VERSION and set it to a specific, compatible patch version. v1.35.0 is only an example of the format. Keep kubectl within one minor version of the API Server. The workflow uses the checksum verification described in the official Linux installation guide.

A one-hour token does not renew itself when stored in a Secret. If it expires, including while waiting for approval, generate a new token and update the Secret. For ongoing production use, exchange a platform-supported OIDC/workload identity for short-lived credentials or use managed rotation. GitHub OIDC tokens are not automatically accepted by every Kubernetes cluster; they need a trust configuration or an identity exchange. See ServiceAccount token documentation.

name: order-api-release

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version: '1.26.9'
          cache: false
      - run: go vet ./...
      - run: go test -race -v ./...
      - name: Check Dockerfile on PR
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: docker build --build-arg VERSION=pr-check -t order-api:pr .

  build:
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - id: name
        shell: bash
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          platforms: linux/amd64
          tags: ${{ steps.name.outputs.image }}:sha-${{ github.sha }}
          build-args: VERSION=${{ github.sha }}
          labels: org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    environment: production
    concurrency:
      group: order-api-production
      cancel-in-progress: false
    env:
      KUBECTL_VERSION: ${{ vars.KUBECTL_VERSION }}
      IMAGE_REF: ${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Install compatible kubectl
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          test -n "$KUBECTL_VERSION"
          url="https://dl.k8s.io/release/${KUBECTL_VERSION}/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
          curl -fsSL "$url" -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/kubectl"
          curl -fsSL "$url.sha256" -o "$RUNNER_TEMP/kubectl.sha256"
          expected=$(cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/kubectl.sha256")
          printf '%s  %s\n' "$expected" "$RUNNER_TEMP/kubectl" | sha256sum --check
          chmod +x "$RUNNER_TEMP/kubectl"
          echo "$RUNNER_TEMP" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"          
      - name: Configure cluster access
        env:
          KUBE_CONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          test -n "$KUBE_CONFIG"
          export KUBECONFIG="$RUNNER_TEMP/order-api.kubeconfig"
          umask 077
          printf '%s' "$KUBE_CONFIG" > "$KUBECONFIG"
          echo "KUBECONFIG=$KUBECONFIG" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n demo-prod | grep -qx yes          
      - name: Reject stale release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          latest=$(gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/git/ref/heads/main" --jq '.object.sha')
          test "$latest" = "$GITHUB_SHA"          
      - name: Save previous Pod template
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          kubectl -n demo-prod get deployment order-api --ignore-not-found -o json \
            | jq -c '.spec.template // empty' > "$RUNNER_TEMP/previous-template.json"          
      - name: Apply release and wait
        id: release
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          kubectl apply -f k8s/runtime.yaml
          kubectl set image --local -f k8s/deployment.yaml \
            "order-api=$IMAGE_REF" -o yaml > "$RUNNER_TEMP/rendered-deployment.yaml"
          kubectl apply -f "$RUNNER_TEMP/rendered-deployment.yaml"
          kubectl -n demo-prod rollout status deployment/order-api --timeout=240s          
      - name: Verify response and source version
        id: verify
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          kubectl -n demo-prod port-forward service/order-api 18080:80 \
            > "$RUNNER_TEMP/port-forward.log" 2>&1 &
          forward_pid=$!
          trap 'kill "$forward_pid" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
          actual=$(curl -fsS --retry 12 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 1 \
            --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:18080/version)
          test "$actual" = "$GITHUB_SHA"
          curl -fsS --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:18080/readyz
          test "$(curl -fsS --max-time 5 http://127.0.0.1:18080/)" = "order-api is running"
          printf 'Verified commit: `%s`\n\nImage: `%s`\n' \
            "$GITHUB_SHA" "$IMAGE_REF" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"          
      - name: Collect failure evidence
        if: ${{ failure() && (steps.release.outcome == 'failure' || steps.verify.outcome == 'failure') }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          kubectl -n demo-prod get deployment,replicaset,pods -l app=order-api -o wide || true
          kubectl -n demo-prod describe deployment order-api || true
          kubectl -n demo-prod get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp || true
          kubectl -n demo-prod logs -l app=order-api --all-containers --prefix --tail=100 || true          
      - name: Restore previous Pod template
        if: ${{ failure() && (steps.release.outcome == 'failure' || steps.verify.outcome == 'failure') }}
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [ ! -s "$RUNNER_TEMP/previous-template.json" ]; then
            echo 'First deployment: no previous template. Manual investigation required.'
            exit 1
          fi
          patch=$(jq -c '[{op:"replace",path:"/spec/template",value:.}]' "$RUNNER_TEMP/previous-template.json")
          kubectl -n demo-prod patch deployment order-api --type=json -p "$patch"
          kubectl -n demo-prod rollout status deployment/order-api --timeout=240s          
      - name: Remove temporary kubeconfig
        if: always()
        shell: bash
        run: rm -f -- "$RUNNER_TEMP/order-api.kubeconfig"

The image publishing setup follows GitHub’s image publishing tutorial and Docker build-push-action. The example uses major Action tags for readability. In production, pin reviewed full commit SHAs and maintain them with dependency updates. A tag such as @v7 can point to a different commit later. Self-hosted Runners must also meet each Action’s runtime requirements.

Design choice Purpose
PRs only run checks; main pushes build and deploy Unmerged code does not receive production deployment credentials
Explicit needs dependencies Failed prerequisites block later stages
Lowercase repository name Produces a valid GHCR path such as ghcr.io/symphonyw/order-api
SHA tag plus deployment by digest Human-readable traceability and an exact artifact identity
context: . Uses the checked-out directory for Docker’s build context
No rebuild during deployment The artifact being released is the one already produced
Local image substitution before apply Avoids deploying the placeholder and applies other Git-managed settings too
Main SHA checked immediately before deployment Reduces the risk of delayed releases overwriting newer work
Deployment concurrency group Prevents overlapping deployment Jobs for this application/environment
Explicit failure() recovery conditions Diagnostics and restoration can run after a failed step

cancel-in-progress: false prevents newer work in the concurrency group from cancelling a running deployment, but GitHub concurrency groups are not strict FIFO release queues. Pending work can be replaced, and execution order is not guaranteed. The main SHA check helps reject stale releases, but another commit can arrive between that check and apply. It is not a transaction lock. This approach suits a “deploy the latest main” policy; strictly ordered releases need a dedicated queue or controller. See GitHub concurrency control.

apply confirms that the API accepted the resources, while rollout status confirms that the controller finished the update. Check the SHA from /version as well to confirm that the responding application is the intended version. The business smoke request then checks more than process health.

Port forwarding a Service selects one Pod and checks its application response. It does not test normal Service forwarding, every replica, DNS, the gateway, or TLS. If a real entry point is available, also check https://your-domain/version and send appropriate business requests through it. One HTTP 200 cannot validate the whole user path.

6. Run a successful release, then rehearse recovery

Step Action Expected result
1 Initialize namespace, RBAC, pull Secret, and production environment Deployer authorization returns yes
2 Commit application files and open a PR Tests and Dockerfile build pass
3 Require the test check for main, then merge Build produces SHA tag and image digest
4 Check first-publish package access The pull account can read the package; pause approval and fix it if necessary
5 Approve production if configured Deploy updates the application using that digest
6 Inspect Workflow Summary and the cluster Source SHA matches and two replicas are available

If the package already exists, check that the repository’s Actions are allowed to write to it. Available branch and environment protections depend on repository type and organizational policies.

After one successful release, rehearse a failure in the dedicated exercise environment only. Change the readiness path to /not-ready, pass the PR checks, and merge. The application returns 404 at that path, leaving the new Pods unready. When the rollout fails, CI collects diagnostic information and restores the saved Pod template. Once you have observed recovery, immediately submit a fix that changes the path back to /readyz so Git is correct too.

The snapshot preserves the template that was running before deployment, which may differ from the previous rollout history entry. Restoring it has the following limits:

Situation Example behavior Additional action
Tests or image build fail Cluster unchanged Fix source and retry
Authentication, permission, or stale-release check fails No apply performed Fix access or release the current commit
New Pods fail and an old template exists Restore template and wait for rollout Validate business behavior and the external path
First deployment fails Explicit failure, no old template Investigate and clean failed resources if necessary
Recovery rollout also times out Job stays failed Operator intervention
Runner disappears, Job is cancelled, or API is unreachable Recovery may not execute Independent monitoring and operational response
Service changed, Secret overwritten, or database migrated Template restoration is insufficient Separate configuration/data recovery strategy

The workflow stays failed even if restoration succeeds. Recovery is an attempt to restore service, not evidence that the release passed. Check business behavior and metrics after the recovery rollout as well. Deployment history rollback restores a Pod template; it does not reverse an entire application transaction. See the Deployment documentation.

Symptom Check first Useful evidence
GHCR push returns 403 Package permissions, repository association, organization policy Build logs and package access settings
Unauthorized / Forbidden Expiration, context, RoleBinding Authorization checks and API response
API connection timeout Runner network, endpoint, firewall, CA Connection errors; never print full kubeconfig
ImagePullBackOff Digest existence, pull credentials, node egress kubectl describe pod <pod> -n demo-prod
Pending Pods Resource requests, amd64 node selector, quotas Scheduling events
CrashLoopBackOff Startup, configuration, permissions, OOM kubectl logs <pod> -p -n demo-prod
Running but not Ready Probe path, listening address, dependencies Pod description and application logs
Internal checks pass but domain fails Controller, Service, DNS, TLS Gateway logs and real entry-point requests

Plan database migrations separately. A common approach is to expand, migrate, then contract: add backward-compatible structures so old and new application versions can run, migrate the data, observe the results, and only then remove the old structures. Migration Jobs need idempotency, concurrency control, and failure handling. Do not let every application Pod race to execute irreversible DDL at startup. Restoring an image does not undo messages already sent, external calls, or changes to records.

7. Evolve toward a maintainable release system

Once the basic workflow works, add the checks and release controls the workload needs.

Area Starting point here Production evolution
Environments Dedicated exercise namespace Isolated dev/staging/prod and production identities
Artifacts SHA tag and digest History retention, scanning, SBOM, signature verification
Credentials Short-lived exercise kubeconfig Per-Job identity exchange, rotation, audit
Validation Readiness, source version, one business request Integration tests, external E2E, environment acceptance
Observation Failure logs and manual checks Error rate, P95/P99 latency, restarts, business indicators, alerts
Release policy Two-replica rolling update Canary or blue/green where risk justifies it
Records SHA, digest, Actions execution Environment, config versions, approvals, recovery outcome

Use the same digest across environments: build once, validate in staging, then deploy that artifact to production. Supply environment differences through configuration. Rebuilding for each environment can produce different images despite identical version labels.

A standard Deployment replaces replicas gradually without using metrics to decide whether to continue. To send limited traffic to a new version, observe the results, and then increase exposure, you also need traffic control and progressive delivery tooling.

GitOps changes which component performs deployment. In this push example, CI holds an identity that calls the API. With GitOps, an environment repository records the desired state, and Argo CD or Flux reconciles the cluster to it from inside the cluster or a controlled network.

Aspect Push CD in this example GitOps
Cluster changes initiated by CI deployment Job Reconciler
Desired image recorded in Source template plus CI digest output Environment manifests containing the exact digest
Cluster deployment credentials Used by CI Held by the reconciler
Manual drift No continuous correction by default Detection and optional correction
Version recovery Restore snapshot, then fix source Change desired digest in the deployment repository

When using Argo CD automatic sync, update the desired state in Git first. Otherwise, self-healing may undo a manual cluster change and restore the version in Git. Resource pruning also needs an explicit policy. See Argo CD automated sync.

Keep a record of each release’s source commit, artifact, configuration, verification coverage, and recovery target. With those records in place, you can trace what happened as you add more environments, progressive delivery, or GitOps.
